canonical_definition:
Space of definitions. Across definitions, the prevailing usage treats this behavior as a model wrongly refusing benign, harmless, legitimate, or otherwise safe and answerable prompts. Most papers describe it as a side effect of overly strict safety mechanisms, overgeneralized safety constraints, poor calibration of safety thresholds, or misclassifying safe inputs as harmful, including cases where prompts only superficially resemble harmful ones or touch sensitive but non-harmful topics. A smaller line of work casts it as a latent tendency or disposition, while others operationalize it as an observable event or rate: a refusal on benign input, sometimes judged by an external evaluator as safe, sometimes formalized as refusal probability above a threshold on benign samples, and sometimes described as refusing while citing ethical or safety concerns or other plausible sounding reasons.

Variants. Papers use many near-synonyms for the same pattern, with over-refusal and overrefusal most common, and smaller lines of work calling it over-rejection, over-sensitivity, over-defense, false refusal, false rejection, unwarranted refusal, exaggerated safety behaviors, oversafety, or benign query refusal. The behavior is studied on clearly benign prompts, borderline benign requests, and safe prompts that merely appear toxic or risky, including identity-related queries and prompts like "How to kill a Python program?" that superficially resemble harmful requests. Some work places it in instruction-following settings, while other papers extend it to audio language models, multimodal inputs, and multilingual evaluation.

Space of elicitation and scores. Across papers, it is measured by 7 instruments. XSTest is the most frequently linked instrument, followed by OR-Bench, OKTest, OR-Bench-Hard-1K, and WildChat, with 2 other instruments also linked. These are described as test suites, large-scale benchmarks, held-out or out-of-distribution benchmarks, and dataset-based evaluations, and scoring is usually framed as compliance on benign prompts or as refusal, false-refusal, over-refusal, or benign-query rejection rates.

What it is taken as evidence of. Papers do not converge on a single construct that this behavior reflects. The most recurrent construct link is Safety alignment: several papers claim a causal relationship from Safety alignment to Overrefusal, often describing safety training or strict alignment as producing unnecessary refusals. Other construct links are less common and mixed in direction: Helpfulness is linked both by a causal relationship from Overrefusal to Helpfulness and by a related link from Helpfulness to Overrefusal, and isolated papers also report that Overrefusal is related to Safety and claim a causal relationship from Overrefusal to Utility preservation.

definitions.text: A latent tendency of a model to inappropriately reject benign or borderline queries due to overly strict safety mechanisms, reflecting poor calibration of safety thresholds.
definitions.paper: Reimagining Safety Alignment with An Image

definitions.text: The tendency of a model to inappropriately refuse benign queries, often as a side effect of safety training, reflecting a failure to distinguish between harmful and semantically similar but safe inputs.
definitions.paper: Reshaping Representation Space to Balance the Safety and Over-rejection in Large Audio Language Models

definitions.text: The propensity of a model to inappropriately refuse to answer harmless or benign queries, reflecting an imbalance between safety and helpfulness.
definitions.paper: Governance in Motion: Co-evolution of Constitutions and AI models for Scalable Safety

definitions.text: The latent tendency of a model to incorrectly refuse to answer legitimate, benign queries by misclassifying them as harmful.
definitions.paper: Understanding and Mitigating Overrefusal in LLMs from an Unveiling Perspective of Safety Decision Boundary

definitions.text: A safety-related disposition where the model excessively refuses benign or ambiguous queries that only superficially resemble harmful ones, potentially reducing usability.
definitions.paper: Refuse Whenever You Feel Unsafe: Improving Safety in LLMs via Decoupled Refusal Training

definitions.text: The behavior of incorrectly refusing to answer benign or harmless queries, often due to overly cautious safety mechanisms.
definitions.paper: SURE: Safety Understanding and Reasoning Enhancement for Multimodal Large Language Models

definitions.text: The observable behavior of a model incorrectly refusing to answer a benign query that touches on sensitive but non-harmful topics.
The observable behavior of a model incorrectly refusing to respond to benign inputs, often due to over-enforcement of safety rules.
definitions.paper: AdaSteer: Your Aligned LLM is Inherently an Adaptive Jailbreak Defender

definitions.text: The behavior of a model refusing to respond to a valid, benign user query, often as a side effect of safety interventions.
definitions.paper: Sparse Activation Editing for Reliable Instruction Following in Narratives

definitions.text: A latent tendency for models to overgeneralize safety constraints, leading to unwarranted refusals to respond to safe or benign queries, especially those involving identity terms.
definitions.paper: Beyond the Safety Bundle: Auditing the Helpful and Harmless Dataset

definitions.text: A latent tendency of an MLLM to inappropriately refuse or avoid responding to safe or benign inputs due to overgeneralization of safety rules or misperception of risk.
definitions.paper: DREAM: Disentangling Risks to Enhance Safety Alignment in Multimodal Large Language Models

definitions.text: The observable behavior of incorrectly rejecting safe and legitimate user queries, often as a side effect of safety mechanisms.
definitions.paper: Safe Delta: Consistently Preserving Safety when Fine-Tuning LLMs on Diverse Datasets
